question: In 1999, the Council provided the Commission with a mandate to negotiate an association agreement with Mercosur. According to the negotiating directive, the agreement was to be a ‘political and economic association agreement ... [which] will constitute a single covenant’. In its conclusions of 22 May 2018, the Council reiterated that this agreement would remain ‘mixed’ and that ‘it is ... for the Council to decide, on a case-by-case basis, on the splitting of trade agreements’. 1.

Many Member States had reservations about the negotiated text. In light of this, how does the Commission justify its intention to assume responsibility for the trade component of the agreement – a competence which falls exclusively to the EU – and the resulting circumvention of the process of adopting a mixed agreement, a process which requires Council unanimity and ratification by the national parliaments?

Does this split point to the Commission taking a position that goes against the spirit of sincere cooperation, and by splitting the agreement, is the Commission not running the risk of further exacerbating public distrust of the European institutions?
Given the rocky geopolitical climate, what adjustments is the Commission making when concluding such trade agreements?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.12.2025) The legal architecture consisting of two parallel legal instruments (the EU-Mercosur Partnership Agreement1 and the Interim Trade Agreement2) is in line with the Treaties. The negotiating directives adopted by the Council in 1999 envisaged the possibility of a separate EU only interim agreement on trade.

This architecture is not new as it was adopted by the Council and the European Parliament for the Advanced Framework Agreement between Chile and the EU3. In line with the Treaties, the Council and the European Parliament will endorse the agreement and ensure legitimacy and inclusiveness of the adoption process.

Trade agreements are concluded by the EU with the consent of the European Parliament, directly elected by EU citizens. These agreements are subject to a vote by the Council, which democratically represents EU governments. Member States represented in the Council may consult with their national parliaments and other stakeholders ahead of the conclusion of the agreement.

The Commission supports Member States’ efforts to inform and consult their national and regional parliaments about the agreement. The Commission also regularly replies to questions from national parliaments.

The Court of Justice4 has clarified the scope of the EU’s exclusive competence in trade policy and confirmed that for matters falling within the EU’s exclusive competence, the power to conclude these agreements belongs to the EU institutions - the Council and the European Parliament.
